index.html: Neural Codes, Noise, and Memory: A Guide to Three Papers These three neuroscience papers study how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The guide connects mathematical models of stored values with eye-movement recordings from monkeys and recordings of spatial activity in rodents and bats. Begin with the reading path for the setting, contribution, and limits of each study, followed by the background and step-by-step calculations. Contents Front matter What the three papers establish These neuroscience papers study memory, eye control, and navigation. Their settings are mathematical models of stored values, eye-movement and neural recordings from macaque monkeys, and recordings of location-dependent neural activity in rodents and bats. This reading guide explains each study’s question, methods, findings, and limits. Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models In a model neural circuit, the pattern of firing rates across many nerve cells can represent a remembered angle. Random spike timing can change that angle even while the circuit sustains its activity. Chapters 1–2 explain neural signals and how activity stores a value. Chapters 3–4 derive how that value wanders over time. Chapters 5–6 connect its stability to how accurately it can be estimated from the cells’ spikes. Chapter 1: Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value Nerve cells communicate with brief electrical spikes. This chapter explains how firing rates across a group of cells can represent an eye angle or an animal’s location, and how variable spike timing affects that representation. These ideas supply the biological and probability background for the three papers. Chapter 2: Stable representations can accumulate error A neural circuit can sustain its firing while the value represented by that firing changes. Using eye angle as an example, this chapter separates changes in the activity of the cells from changes in the stored value. That distinction explains how persistent activity can still accumulate memory error. Chapter 3: Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor Burak and Fiete model a group of interacting neurons that retains a continuous value after an input ends. This chapter follows spikes through their effects at synapses and back into firing, then derives how random spike timing displaces the stored value. Chapter 4: Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays In the memory-network model, random changes in a stored angle accumulate over time. This chapter extends the local spreading calculation to longer delays, where boundaries, angular wraparound, and systematic drift can change the size of the memory error. Chapter 5: Spike information limits memory stability A neuron receiving spikes from a memory circuit has access to information about the stored value. This chapter sets a bound on estimation error under the model’s assumptions and derives the constraint that spike information places on the circuit’s memory stability. Chapter 6: Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement. Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code The next studies connect neural activity to eye control in monkeys and to location in rodents and bats. Chapters 7–9 follow the path from a neural command through eye muscles to measured movement, and test a possible source of drift. Chapters 10–12 explain where hippocampal nerve cells fire as an animal moves and compare a spatial model with recordings. Chapter 13 asks what these findings establish together and which connections remain untested. Chapter 7: Eye drift points to a shared neural drive Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism. Chapter 8: Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error. Chapter 9: A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift A circuit that stores the intended eye angle is one possible source of fixational drift. This chapter follows the proposed model from interacting neurons through motor neurons and muscles to eye motion, and explains how delayed visual feedback can limit that motion. Chapter 10: Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell. Chapter 11: High peaks explain size laws across dimensions A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation. Chapter 12: Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation Recordings show where a hippocampal cell is active as an animal moves through an environment. This chapter tests the spatial model against the shapes and arrangement of those regions, then asks what agreement can reveal about the inputs and connections that produce them. Chapter 13: Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests The three papers address different links between nerve-cell activity and behavior: retaining a value, producing eye movement, and representing location. This chapter compares what the models and recordings establish, and separates supported connections from further questions about how a complete neural circuit would work. appendices/ch-glossary.html: AppendicesGlossary Glossary These short definitions support lookup after the explanations and examples in the main chapters. abducens nucleus: A brainstem group containing the motor neurons recorded in the eye-drift study; their axons activate the lateral rectus eye muscle. activity bump: A localized peak of population firing rates across neurons ordered by their preferred represented values. attractor manifold: The continuous family of persistent activity states, described by its represented coordinates rather than by every neural activity separately. Betti numbers: Counts of independent connected components, loops, cavities, and their higher-dimensional counterparts. Brownian motion: A continuous random process starting at zero with independent Gaussian increments of mean zero and variance equal to elapsed time. causal filter: A rule whose current output depends only on present and past input. coefficient of determination: For the optimal linear prediction with an intercept, the fraction of response variance removed by prediction; with one predictor it equals the squared correlation. coefficient of variation: Standard deviation divided by mean; in the spike-train discussion it is applied to interspike intervals. continuous attractor: A continuous family of fixed points with restoring dynamics toward the family and neutral motion along it in the ideal deterministic model. convolution: An integral or sum combining past input values with a shifted response kernel to obtain a filtered output. correlation coefficient: Covariance divided by the product of standard deviations; a dimensionless measure of linear association. covariance: The mean product of two centered random variables, measuring their shared variation. Cramér Rao bound: A lower bound on local unbiased estimation variance under the required regularity conditions, expressed through inverse Fisher information. critical point: A point where a function’s gradient is zero. The Euler calculation also requires invertible Hessians. decoding: Estimating a represented value from neural responses. dendrite: A branching input structure of a neuron. diffusion coefficient: The coefficient \(D\) in the local one-dimensional displacement variance \(2Dt\); its units are coordinate squared per time. diffusion tensor: The matrix giving local coordinate-displacement covariances per twice the elapsed time. Dirac delta: A point-mass distribution; in the initial-condition equation all probability is concentrated at the specified coordinate. encoding: Establishing a population activity pattern from an input. Euler characteristic: The alternating sum of Betti numbers; in three dimensions, components minus independent loops plus enclosed cavities. excess kurtosis: The fourth centered moment divided by the squared variance, minus three. It is zero for a Gaussian population. excitatory input: In the models used here, an input that increases a receiving neuron’s tendency to fire. excursion set: The positions where a function exceeds a specified level. Fano factor: Spike-count variance divided by mean count, for a specified counting interval and condition. firing rate: The expected number of spikes per unit time, conditional on the modeled circumstances. Fisher information: The expected squared score, quantifying the local sensitivity of a probability distribution to a parameter. fixational drift: Slow eye motion during attempted fixation, between rapid eye movements. fixed point: A state whose deterministic rate of change is zero. Fokker Planck equation: An equation describing how a probability density evolves under drift and diffusion; the guide states the convention before using it. gain: The scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in another. gamma function: The function \(\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du\) for \(t>0\), extending factorials through \(\Gamma(n+1)=n!\). Gaussian curvature: For a surface in three dimensions, the product of its two principal curvatures. Gaussian process: A distribution over functions whose values at any finite collection of positions have a joint Gaussian distribution. grid cell: A spatially tuned entorhinal neuron with repeated firing fields, often approximately hexagonally arranged in a two-dimensional arena. Hessian: The matrix of second derivatives of a function with respect to its coordinates. hippocampus: A brain region involved in memory and navigation. hyperbolic cotangent: The function \(\coth z=1/\tanh z\), for real \(z\ne0\). hyperbolic tangent: The function \(\tanh z=(e^z-e^{-z})/(e^z+e^{-z})\). impulse response: The output of a linear filter in response to a unit-area input impulse, from which responses to general input can be assembled. inhibitory input: In the models used here, an input that reduces a receiving neuron’s tendency to fire. internal Fisher information rate: The local information per unit observation time about the instantaneous attractor coordinate, as defined by the 2012 spike model. inverse hyperbolic tangent: The inverse of \(\tanh\) on \((-1,1)\), given by \(\operatorname{artanh}z=\tfrac12\log[(1+z)/(1-z)]\). Isotropy: Invariance of the spatial probability law under rotations. Itô convention: A stochastic-increment convention that evaluates the noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment. jointly Gaussian vector: A random vector for which every linear combination of its entries is Gaussian. Kac–Rice formula: A way to compute expected crossing or critical-point counts from the joint distribution of a random function and its derivatives, under the relevant regularity assumptions. left zero eigenvector: A vector \(v\) with \(v^T A=0\); with appropriate normalization it extracts the persistent coordinate from a small state disturbance. likelihood: The probability or density of the observed data considered as a function of a proposed parameter value. linearization: The first-order approximation to a dynamical equation near a reference state. lognormal distribution: A distribution of positive values whose logarithms are Gaussian. low pass filter: A filter that suppresses sufficiently rapid input changes relative to slower ones. mean curvature: For a surface in three dimensions, the average of its two principal curvatures. mean squared displacement: The average squared change in a coordinate across a specified time lag. microsaccades: Brief, rapid eye movements that occur during attempted fixation. Morse theory: A theory relating the topology of a function’s level-set regions to its critical points. The guide uses a signed critical-point count under its smoothness and nondegeneracy assumptions, including boundary contributions. neural transfer function: The modeled relationship between a neuron’s input and its expected firing rate. neuron: A signaling cell in the nervous system. ocular motoneurons (OMNs): Neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles. ocular plant: The muscles and mechanical eye system that transform motor activity into eye motion. oculomotor integrator: A neural circuit that converts movement commands into a maintained eye-position command. p value: Under the specified null comparison, the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme in the tested direction as the observed one. path integration: Updating an estimate of position from movement. place cell: A spatially selective hippocampal neuron that fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. place field: A connected region of elevated spatial firing, as defined by the model or stated measurement procedure. Poisson process: A counting process with independent increments and a deterministic constant or time-dependent event rate; its count over an interval has equal mean and variance. In a recurrent model, conditionally Poisson instantaneous spike generation does not make complete spike trains have independent increments. population code: A representation carried by the pattern of responses across neurons. precision: The reciprocal of variance for a scalar Gaussian estimate. preferred angle: An angle where a neuron’s tuning curve peaks. prior distribution: A distribution representing knowledge about likely parameter values before observing the current data. rate map: An estimate of spatial firing rate from spikes per time spent at each position. Rayleigh distribution: The distribution of a positive variable that is a scaled square root of an exponential variable. recurrent connectivity: Connections that feed activity back into the same neuronal population. renewal process: An event process with independent, identically distributed intervals under the fixed conditions being modeled. retina: The light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. right zero eigenvector: A state-space direction \(u\) satisfying \(Au=0\) for the linearized dynamics. root mean squared displacement: The square root of mean squared displacement, expressed in the original coordinate’s units. score: The derivative of log likelihood with respect to the parameter being estimated. skew: The third centered moment divided by the variance to the power \(3/2\), measuring asymmetry. Smoothness: The existence and regularity of derivatives of a function. The crossing and peak calculations require different derivative orders. spike: A brief electrical event emitted by a neuron. standard error of the mean (SEM): An estimate of uncertainty in a sample mean. Its interpretation depends on which observations are treated as independent, such as trials, cells, or animals. state: The quantities that specify a modeled system’s current condition and determine its subsequent dynamics together with future inputs and noise. Stationarity: In the place-field model, invariance of spatial statistics under translating the map. stationary process: A random process whose probability law is unchanged by shifting its time or position origin; weaker covariance-only stationarity must be specified when used. Stratonovich convention: A stochastic-increment convention using midpoint evaluation in the limiting increments. sub-Poisson spiking: Spiking with less variability than a matched Poisson reference according to the stated measure and conditions. superdiffusion: Mean squared displacement growing faster than linearly with lag over the range being described. synapse: A connection through which one neuron influences another. systematic drift: A nonzero mean velocity of the represented coordinate, distinct from random spreading. Translation invariance: In the readout model, invariance under shifts of the represented value. It makes the readout variance independent of the cue state. tuning curve: A neuron’s expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable. unbiased: Describes an estimator whose expected value equals the parameter locally under the conditions used in the estimation bound. upcrossing: A point where a function crosses upward through a specified threshold. weak fluctuation approximation: An expansion about the deterministic population dynamics in which the aggregate effects of many small spike contributions remain small. Weibull distribution: A positive-variable distribution with survival probability \(\exp[-(s/b)^k]\), scale \(b>0\), and shape \(k>0\). White noise: An ideal noise input with zero covariance at unequal times and a delta-function covariance at equal times; its integrated increments have finite variance.

chapters/ch-eye-circuit.html: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code9 A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift 9 A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift A circuit that stores the intended eye angle is one possible source of fixational drift. This chapter follows the proposed model from interacting neurons through motor neurons and muscles to eye motion, and explains how delayed visual feedback can limit that motion. The recordings support a shared source before the motor neurons, and the movement’s timing is compatible with a stored position that wanders. Neither result identifies the circuit that supplies that command. A noisy memory circuit is a proposed explanation whose output must pass through the motor neurons and muscles before it can be compared with eye movement. Following that complete path lets the model test whether neural noise can produce both the amount and timing of the observed drift. Its spike variability, neuron count and time constants determine how much freedom this match allows. Comparing the model with the separate recording and timing results then shows what the study supports, and why it still leaves other upstream sources possible. 9.1 A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. The model has two groups of integrator neurons. One group fires more when the eye points farther right; the other fires more when it points farther left. Neurons excite cells in their own group and inhibit cells in the other group. The connection strengths are tuned so that the circuit can approximately maintain a range of represented eye positions.1 For the right population, the model’s rate is \[ \lambda_i^R(t)=\left[\zeta_i^R E_{OI}(t)+\lambda_i^0+\zeta_i^R F(t)\right]_+, \qquad [a]_+=\max(a,0). \] \(E_{OI}\) is the internally represented position in degrees, \(\zeta_i^R\) is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and \(\lambda_i^0\) is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. \(F\) is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, \(\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R\). In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by \(\zeta_i\). The model scales each spike train into an input \(X_i\) with a saturating mean response. This input changes the neuron’s synaptic output \(S_i\), the lingering effect of its spikes on neurons receiving them. A weighted difference between the two groups’ synaptic outputs gives the represented eye angle \(E_{OI}\). This value sets the firing rates again, closing the feedback loop: \[ \tau_s\dot S_i^R=-S_i^R+X_i^R,\qquad X_i^R(t)=\frac{\xi_i^R(t)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(t)},\qquad E_{OI}(t)=\sum_i\eta_i[S_i^R(t)-S_i^L(t)]. \] Here \(\xi_i^R\) is a spike train generated at rate \(\lambda_i^R\), \(\tau_s\) is the synaptic decay time, and \(\lambda_t=60\) Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, \(X_i\) and \(S_i\) are dimensionless, and the weights \(\eta_i\) are in degrees. Between spikes, \(S_i\) decays exponentially; one spike adds a jump of \(1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]\). Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive \(\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)\) that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model’s saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.2 Persistence requires a further condition on that feedback. Set \(F=0\) and replace spikes by their mean rates. Define the mean saturated drives at a proposed stored value \(z\) by \[ q_i^R(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^R(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(z)}, \qquad q_i^L(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^L(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^L(z)}. \] Multiply each synaptic equation by its readout weight, subtract the left contribution, and sum. Since the same \(\tau_s\) applies to every unit, the readout obeys \[ \tau_s\dot E_{OI}=-E_{OI}+G(E_{OI}), \qquad G(z)=\sum_i\eta_i[q_i^R(z)-q_i^L(z)]. \] An exact continuum of persistent readout values would require \(G(z)=z\) over the represented range. For a small displacement from a fixed value, Taylor expansion gives \[ \tau_s\,\frac{d\,\delta E_{OI}}{dt} =[G'(z)-1]\delta E_{OI}. \] Thus \(G'(z)=1\) is the local neutral condition for the stored coordinate. Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across \(-50\) to \(50\) degrees. Residual mismatch can produce deterministic drift, so this finite optimized circuit provides approximate persistence rather than an exactly neutral continuum. The tuning slopes and thresholds were sampled to match reported macaque relationships and variation. With spikes, perturbations along the nearly neutral direction additionally accumulate. This reduction is a teaching derivation from the paper’s equations; Figure 4 separates the resulting internal diffusion from later muscle smoothing.3 The motor neurons receive this position signal: \[ \lambda_i^M(t)=[k_i(E_{OI}(t)-E_{T_i})]_+, \qquad \tau_{MN}\dot s_i^M=-s_i^M+\xi_i^M. \] \(\lambda_i^M\) is a motor rate in spikes/s, \(E_{T_i}\) is that neuron’s position threshold in degrees, and \(k_i\) is its position sensitivity. \(\xi_i^M\) is its generated spike train. The filtered output \(s_i^M\) also has units spikes/s, with decay time \(\tau_{MN}\). One spike makes a jump of \(1/\tau_{MN}\); at constant mean rate, the mean output is that rate. Each motor unit’s muscle and plant response is represented by a position contribution \(E_i\) satisfying \[ s_i^M=k_i(E_i-E_{T_i})+r_i\dot E_i+m_i\ddot E_i, \qquad E=\frac1{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}E_i. \] These are Eqs. 28–31. The second order equation uses the same roles and units as the forward fit. At constant \(E_{OI}\), an active unit has mean \(s_i^M=k_i(E_{OI}-E_{T_i})\), giving mean \(E_i=E_{OI}\) when derivatives vanish. Averaging therefore transmits the common position while reducing independent private fluctuations. This is an effective model of combined motor output, not a claim that one motor unit moves an isolated eye of its own.4 The model used diverse thresholds and response coefficients, with motor thresholds sampled between \(-45\) and \(-5\) degrees, and imposed \(m_i<r_i^2/(4k_i)\) to give nonoscillatory individual response kernels. Main Methods report \(N=30{,}000\) integrator neurons, \(N_m=1{,}000\) OMNs, and \(\tau_s=20\) ms for the main full simulation. The separate private OMN comparison in Fig. 3 used 2,000 OMNs. These neuron counts belong to different simulation comparisons.5 As the eye moves while viewing a stationary target, the target’s image moves across the retina. The authors assume that visual feedback responds to this recent image motion rather than to an absolute target-position error. Their delayed feedback model is: \[ F(t)=A[E(t-\tau_d)-E_{OI}(t)], \qquad \tau_d\simeq70\ \text{ms}. \] Both positions are in degrees, so \(A\) is dimensionless in this formulation. The main value is \(A=0.015\). If gaze and its internal representation have recently moved rightward, the delayed position is to their left, making \(F\) negative. Its contribution to the integrator rates then opposes continued rightward movement. For a slowly varying position that the eye tracks, \(E(t-\tau_d)-E_{OI}(t)\simeq-\tau_d\dot E(t)\), showing the velocity-like action and sign. The approximation requires tracking and slow change over the delay.6 The effect on the ongoing MSD must be checked from the coupled model, rather than inferred from the delay alone. A short MSD lag is a separation between two samples in a running process, not the time since a new perturbation. Past measurements can already affect both samples, and \(F\) also contains the immediate term \(-A E_{OI}(t)\). Extended Data Fig. 3 compares the model with and without feedback: feedback changes amplitude across lags, while its larger effect on logarithmic slope occurs at longer lags. Figure 5 shows the full model. Muscle filtering supplies the short-lag smoothness, and feedback improves the detailed longer-lag fit. These are results of this model comparison, not a hard delay-based cutoff or a claim excluding visual control under other tasks.7 9.2 Spike regularity and circuit parameters set the model’s drift scale An agreement in amplitude is informative only if we know how much freedom the model has. The paper uses regular spike trains. The spike variability section defined the interspike interval coefficient of variation (CV) as the interval standard deviation divided by its mean. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one; the model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. Such firing is called sub-Poisson spiking here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.8 The construction starts with a Poisson process at \(M\) times the desired rate and retains every \(M\)th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of \(M\) independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean \(1/(M\lambda)\) and variance \(1/(M\lambda)^2\). The retained interval therefore has mean \(1/\lambda\), variance \(1/(M\lambda^2)\), and CV \(1/\sqrt M\). This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model; the simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate. At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. This is a renewal process, a spike process whose successive intervals are independent and identically distributed. Let their mean be \(\mu=1/\lambda\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_I\). The time to \(n\) spikes has variance \(n\sigma_I^2\). For a long fixed window \(L\simeq n\mu\), a fluctuation in total interval time produces the opposite fluctuation in count divided by \(\mu\). Thus \[ \operatorname{Var}(n)\simeq\frac{n\sigma_I^2}{\mu^2} \simeq\lambda L\left(\frac{\sigma_I}{\mu}\right)^2 =\lambda L\,\mathrm{CV}^2. \] This explains why the diffusion scale contains CV squared: it is the strength of the accumulated spike fluctuations relative to the Poisson case. The diffusion calculation and information bound show how projecting those fluctuations onto a neutral memory direction adds a factor proportional to \(1/\tau_s^2\) and, for a comparable independent population, \(1/N\). Rate and sensitivity need more care. Write the absolute local rate slope as \(a=d\lambda/dE\), in spikes/(s deg). If \(N\) similar cells fire near rate \(\lambda_0\), their Poisson information per unit time about position is \[ J\simeq\frac{Na^2}{\lambda_0}. \] Using the information-diffusion relation as a scale, including the \(\mathrm{CV}^2\) factor just derived and holding the network geometry fixed, \[ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{\tau_s^2J} =\frac{\mathrm{CV}^2\lambda_0}{N a^2\tau_s^2}. \] If instead sensitivity is expressed as the fractional slope \(b=a/\lambda_0\), in inverse degrees, the same expression becomes \[ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{N\lambda_0 b^2\tau_s^2}. \] This second form has the dependence printed in the paper’s Eq. 1, \(D\propto\mathrm{CV}^2N^{-1}\lambda_0^{-1}k_0^{-2}\tau_s^{-2}\). However, its surrounding text calls \(k_0\) position sensitivity without specifying fractional normalization. If \(k_0\) means an absolute slope in Hz/degree, that printed expression has the wrong units for \(D\); the version with \(\lambda_0\) in the numerator has the required units deg\(^2\)/s. This scaling is a comparison under fixed network geometry and noise assumptions, not an exact formula for every recurrent circuit.9 At fixed network geometry and under the noise assumptions above, the scale changes as follows: Doubling \(N\) halves it. Doubling CV multiplies it by four. Doubling \(\tau_s\) divides it by four. Doubling the absolute slope at fixed rate also divides it by four. Increasing rate reduces diffusion when the fractional slope is fixed, because more spikes then also supply a proportionally steeper absolute slope. Increasing rate at fixed absolute slope is a different comparison and increases the scale in the first formula. A rate change alone does not specify which comparison is intended. Could the measured CV itself mostly reflect drift rather than private spike variability? Supplementary Notes test this. Let \(\lambda(t)=\bar\lambda+aB(t)\) during a fixation of length \(T\), with the rate changes small relative to \(\bar\lambda\). For a Brownian path starting at zero, the expected time averaged squared position is \(DT\), and the expected squared time mean is \(2DT/3\). Subtracting gives the expected within-segment position variance \(DT/3=2DT/6\): \[ \mathbb E\!\left[\frac1T\int_0^T(B(t)-\bar B)^2dt\right] =\frac{DT}{3}. \] The second term follows from \(\mathbb E[B(t)B(s)]=2D\min(t,s)\) and \(T^{-2}\int_0^T\int_0^T2D\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds=2DT/3\). chapters/ch-eye-drift.html: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code7 Eye drift points to a shared neural drive 7 Eye drift points to a shared neural drive Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism. Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called microsaccades, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.1 This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye’s movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. 7.1 From stored eye position to muscle action The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The oculomotor integrator is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the foundations and network model stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.2 The signal reaches ocular motoneurons (OMNs), neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles. The recordings came from the abducens nucleus, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types using their eye movement response parameters. Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the ocular plant, turn neural activity into movement.3 There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. Private spike variability in individual OMNs. Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging. This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. 7.2 The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye’s angle while an electrode recorded one neuron’s spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement; there were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.45 The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals; they do not create 57 independent animal samples.6 The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell’s activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other. The diagram separates the physical pathway from the paired recordings and the later calculation of predicted eye position. Figure 7.1: The recordings pair one motor neuron with eye movement. Private spike variability acts at individual cells, downstream physical variability acts on movement, and measurement noise enters the eye-position record. The attractor storage source is proposed; the dashed analysis path is a calculation from one cell through its calibrated filter. Original guide schematic based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figs. 1–2 and 4–5. Signal symbols are illustrative, not experimental traces. The upper path describes a possible physical source and its output. The recording design provides one cell and eye movement at a time; it does not measure covariance between simultaneously recorded motor neurons. The predicted position is a later analysis result, not a signal sent backward through the physical pathway. 7.3 A fitted model links movement to firing rate Position alone does not predict a motor neuron’s activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits \[ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). \] Here \(E\) is horizontal eye position in degrees and \(\widehat f\) is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold \(E_T\) sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units \[ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. \] Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. The delay \(\Delta t\) is in seconds: firing at time \(t\) predicts movement at the later time \(t+\Delta t\) for a positive neural lead. This is the paper’s Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.7 The observed rate \(f(t)\) was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors, \[ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. \] \(a\) labels trials and \(T_a\) is trial duration. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial’s rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.8 During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment’s mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell; Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. Its p value is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed. Across 57 cells it gave \(p=3\times10^{-9}\). A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.9 7.4 A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell’s spikes To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell’s spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals. Let \(x(t)=E(t)-E_T\). Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is \[ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. \] A causal filter computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its impulse response \(h_0(u)\) is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero. To factor the equation, consider a time component \(e^{pt}\): differentiation multiplies it by \(p\). The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is \[ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. \] Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times \[ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. \] These are the paired signs in the paper’s Eq. 7, with \(\tau_+>\tau_-\) when \(k,r,m>0\) and \(r^2>4km\). In this case both components decay without oscillation. The same factorization gives two useful identities: \[ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. \] The corresponding impulse response is \[ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). \] \(\Theta(u)\) is zero for \(u<0\) and one for \(u>0\); it imposes causality. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: \(h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)\). Write the spike train as \(\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)\), where \(\delta\) is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. The prediction is \[ \widehat E(t)=E_T+\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(t-v)\xi(v)\,dv =E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j). \] These expressions reproduce Eqs. 4–6, including the factor \(\tau_+\tau_-/m\) and the delay. The convolution integral adds the responses to all past spikes. With spike count treated as a count, \(\xi\) has units spikes/s and \(h\) has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response; adding those responses produces degrees.10 Derivation: the weights of the two decaying responses We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as \[ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. \] To find \(A\) and \(B\), treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so \(h_0(0^+)=0\). Integrating \(m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0\) across the pulse gives \(m h_0'(0^+)=1\): the velocity changes by \(1/m\), while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore \[ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. \] Substituting \(B=-A\) gives \(A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m\), hence \(A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]\). Making the response zero before the spike gives the impulse response \(h_0(u)\). For a constructed example, take \(k=4\) spikes/(s deg), \(\tau_+=0.120\) s, and \(\tau_-=0.005\) s. The identities above require \(r=0.500\) spikes/deg and \(m=0.00240\) spikes s/deg. Then \[ h_0(u)=2.174\left(e^{-u/0.120}-e^{-u/0.005}\right) \ \text{deg/spike},\quad u>0, \] and its area is \(2.174(0.120-0.005)=0.250\) deg s/spike, equal to \(1/k\). A steady rate of 80 spikes/s predicts an offset of 20 degrees above \(E_T\). This checks the gain as well as the time constants; it is not a fit to a recorded cell. Check: static gain and equal decay times The kernel’s area checks its normalization: \[ \int_0^\infty h_0(u)\,du =\frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(\tau_+-\tau_-) =\frac1k. \] Thus a constant input rate \(f_0\) predicts \(E_T+f_0/k\), exactly the static forward relation. A kernel with unit area would give the wrong conversion unless \(k\) had already been absorbed into the input. When the two decay times coincide, \(r^2=4km\), the limit is \(h_0(u)=\Theta(u)u e^{-u/\tau}/m\). The distinct exponential formula is used for the fitted responses in the paper. Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell’s reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was \(\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02\), where the error is the standard error of the mean (SEM). SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals. The one sided test gave \(p=3.8\times10^{-12}\). Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below \(\langle\cdot\rangle\) over cells means a population average.11 7.5 The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement \(Y\) and one centered prediction \(X\), the best linear prediction \(bX\) minimizes \(\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)\). Differentiating with respect to \(b\) gives \(b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)\). Its explained fraction of variance is \[ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. \] This is the coefficient of determination for a linear prediction with a fitted gain. It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. Suppose there are \(N_m\) independent single neuron predictors \(X_i\). Standardize each to variance one and also standardize \(Y\). Independence makes the \(X_i\) uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance \[ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. \] Consequently \(\sum_iR_i^2\le1\), and an average neuron explains at most \(1/N_m\). This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.12 The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead, \[ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. \] Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%; for several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source. Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.13 This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.14 7.6 Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the fact that the inverse filter has a calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as \[ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, \] where \(C=\delta E_C\) is the common upstream contribution, \(\eta\) combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and \(\epsilon\) is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. \(C,\eta,\epsilon\) are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: \[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). \] The common fraction is therefore estimated by \[ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. \] These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between \(\epsilon\) and \(\eta\), because the recorded neuron’s private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order \(1/N_m\) under its many neuron model.15 Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: \[ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. \] Large private noise in a cell inflates \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) and makes \(R\) small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there. Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82. These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with \[ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. \] Then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820\), all in deg\(^2\). It follows that \[ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. \] One cell explains \(R^2\simeq2.89\%\) of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise. Figure 7.2: The same common variance enters movement and the single cell predictor, but the predictor has much more private noise. Increasing only private predictor variance lowers correlation R while the common movement fraction χ stays at 0.82. The marked point uses the chapter’s constructed example. Calculations assume unit common gain and mutually uncorrelated contributions; they are not recorded cell data. Based on Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main p. 10, Eqs. 11–15. Private prediction noise enlarges the denominator of R without changing the covariance. The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10. In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate \(\chi_i\), and those estimates can lie outside \([0,1]\). The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error \(\Delta\chi_i\) mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: \[ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. \] To see the weighting, let normalized weights \(a_i\) sum to one. Independent errors give variance \(\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2\) for \(\sum_i a_i\chi_i\). Minimizing this subject to \(\sum_i a_i=1\) gives \(a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2\) and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. The reported result was \(0.82\pm0.07\), a weighted mean and weighted error for horizontal displacement over 350 ms. Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code8 Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise 8 Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error. The shared movement estimate concerns a single interval length. It leaves open whether the command merely fluctuates around a stable value or keeps accumulating changes. Comparing displacements over different time separations can distinguish these possibilities, but the smallest measured displacements may include a large contribution from recording error. The mean squared displacement measures the average squared position change over a chosen interval. Separating the recording error from that quantity is necessary before interpreting its growth. To test whether the command accumulates changes, we compare two possible inputs after a decaying muscle response: fluctuations that do not accumulate and a position that wanders by diffusion. Their different long interval behavior explains how a smooth eye movement can still reflect a wandering stored value. 8.1 Independent measurement error adds a constant offset to the MSD The common variance calculation uses one interval length. To learn what kind of process drives motion, the authors next compare displacements at many time separations. Using the earlier definition of mean squared displacement, \[ M(\ell)=\mathbb E\{[E(t+\ell)-E(t)]^2\} \] is the mean squared displacement, or MSD, at lag \(\ell\). The data estimate it within each microsaccade free segment, then average the available segment estimates at each lag. Larger lags have fewer eligible segments. The 1 ms sampling sets the available lag spacing.1 At short lags, the displacement can be smaller than the search coil’s measurement error. Suppose its reading is \(E_{m obs}(t)=E(t)+
u(t)\). The measurement error is assumed to have: Zero mean and variance \(\sigma_m^2\). Independence from true movement. No correlation between distinct sampled times. For a positive lag, \[  egin{aligned} M_{m obs}(\ell) &=\mathbb E[(\delta E+\delta

The correction is the variance of a difference of two errors, \(2\sigma_m^2\), rather than the variance of a single position error. At exactly zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so the MSD is zero. A positive lag plateau near zero lag can still occur when successive measurement errors are independent.2 The authors estimated the plateau contribution at order \(10^{-3}\) deg\(^2\), checked its scale with a coil fixed in space, and subtracted that contribution from the observed MSD. If the plateau estimate has uncertainty \(10^{-4}\) deg\(^2\), a corrected MSD of that size is unreliable even when the plateau itself is much larger. Define that local slope by \[ \alpha(\ell)= rac{d\log M(\ell)}{d\log\ell} = rac{\ell M'(\ell)}{M(\ell)}. \] Ordinary diffusion has \(M=2D\ell\) and \(\alpha=1\). A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement \(v\ell\) and \(M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2\), so \(\alpha=2\). Growth faster than linear is called superdiffusion. Here it describes a finite range of lags; it does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.4 Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? A low pass filter suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones. White noise here is an ideal zero mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. In continuous time its strength is defined by an intensity multiplying a delta function, rather than a finite variance at an individual time. A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a stationary process in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation. Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let \(E=h*\xi\), where \[ \mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t'). \] The noise intensity \(A\) has units input\(^2\) times seconds. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. chapters/ch-foundations.html: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models1 Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value 1 Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value Nerve cells communicate with brief electrical spikes. This chapter explains how firing rates across a group of cells can represent an eye angle or an animal’s location, and how variable spike timing affects that representation. These ideas supply the biological and probability background for the three papers. The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system. The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns. Before asking how a circuit keeps a value, we need to know how its activity represents that value and what makes the activity variable. We begin with the spikes that cells send and the patterns of firing rates across a population. A model of spike counts then shows why one brief observation can be uncertain and how combining counts from several cells can help. We then learn how to tell whether measurements vary together and how to separate random spreading from a change in the average value. Those distinctions will let us interpret both a memory model and measurements of eye motion. 1.1 Patterns of firing rates represent a value A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called spikes. A firing rate is the expected number of spikes per unit time. A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds. Neurons affect one another through connections called synapses. In the models used here, inputs have two contrasting effects: An excitatory input increases a receiving neuron’s tendency to fire. An inhibitory input reduces it. The effect of a spike can last beyond the spike itself because synaptic input decays over time. When neurons send signals back into the same population, the circuit has recurrent connectivity. Such feedback can maintain activity after an external signal disappears. A tuning curve gives a neuron’s expected firing rate as a function of a represented variable. For eye angle \(\theta\), a simple local model is \(r_i(\theta)=b_i+k_i\theta\). Neuron \(i\) has baseline rate \(b_i\) in spikes per second and slope \(k_i\) in spikes per second per degree. The linear expression can describe an active range, but it must be modified where it would predict negative firing. The eye paper includes a firing threshold and terms for movement as well as position.1 Different cells have different tuning curves. The vector \[ \mathbf r(\theta)=\bigl(r_1(\theta),\ldots,r_N(\theta)\bigr) \] is a population code: the pattern across \(N\) neurons carries information about \(\theta\). The position of a cell in this vector is a neuron identity, rather than a location in physical space. Reading a value from observed spikes is decoding. Establishing a population pattern from an input is encoding. The 2012 paper asks how accurately the network can maintain such a pattern using its own noisy activity. Spatial tuning gives a second example. In the hippocampus, a brain structure involved in memory and navigation, a place cell fires strongly in one or more localized regions of an environment. A connected region of elevated spatial firing is a place field. One neuron can have several fields. A rate map estimates the rate at each position by dividing the spikes recorded there by the time spent there. Sparse visits, smoothing, and firing cutoffs therefore affect the estimated map and its fields. A field in a model’s expected rate and a field extracted from finite recordings are related objects with different measurement uncertainties.2 The hippocampal areas CA3 and CA1 contain place cells, but their connections differ: CA3 supplies major input to CA1 and has substantial recurrent excitation. CA1 also receives input from entorhinal cortex and has much less local recurrent excitation. A grid cell, found in entorhinal cortex, has repeated spatial fields that often form an approximately hexagonal pattern in a two-dimensional arena. These repeated grid fields and a place cell’s irregular multiple fields should be kept distinct. A model explaining CA1’s output maps need not identify where the animal’s position estimate is maintained.3 1.2 A variable spike count at a fixed rate A tuning curve describes expected activity, but a brief spike observation can differ each time the same value is represented. The 2012 model describes this variability with a Poisson process. At constant rate \(r\), the number \(K\) of spikes in an interval of length \(\Delta t\) obeys \[ \Pr(K=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}, \qquad \lambda=r\Delta t, \qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots . \] Here \(\lambda\) is an expected count, so it has no units. For this distribution, \[ \mathbb E[K]=\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\lambda. \] Derivation: why a Poisson count has variance equal to its mean Summing \(k\Pr(K=k)\) gives \(\lambda\). Likewise, summing \(k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)\) gives \(\lambda^2\). Since \(K^2=K(K-1)+K\), \[ \mathbb E[K^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(K)=\mathbb E[K^2]-\mathbb E[K]^2=\lambda. \] The count variance grows with rate, while its size relative to the mean falls. Its relative standard deviation is \(\sqrt\lambda/\lambda=1/\sqrt\lambda\). This is why collecting more independent spikes can improve a rate estimate. It also means that increasing a firing-rate scale does not keep absolute noise amplitude fixed. Comparisons between networks must specify which quantities are held constant.4 Example: an apparently silent cell and an informative population Suppose the expected rate is 20 spikes per second and an observation lasts 50 ms. The expected count is \(20\times0.05=1\). The probability of seeing no spike is \(e^{-1}=0.368\). A silent interval is therefore common even though the expected rate is positive. Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation \(\sqrt{20}=4.47\). The total rate estimate has a relative standard deviation of about 22.4%, compared with 100% for one cell. Population averaging helps because the independent count variances add while the mean signal adds directly. If a common varying input makes several cells’ firing rates rise and fall together, that shared variation will not disappear in the same way. The two count distributions can be compared on the same rate per cell scale. Figure 1.1: Analytic teaching construction for the chapter’s 20 Hz, 50 ms example. The count is Poisson with mean 1 for one cell and mean 20 for 20 conditionally independent cells. Both panels plot the rate per cell \(K/(N\Delta t)\), so both estimates have mean 20 Hz; their standard deviations are 20 Hz and 4.47 Hz. Each stem is a probability at one possible estimate, rather than a continuous density. Only estimates through 100 Hz are drawn. The independence condition concerns fixed modeled rates, not complete recurrent spike trains. Dividing the pooled rate estimate by 20 keeps the expected rate per cell fixed, while independent averaging reduces its relative spread. See Poisson count likelihood, SI Eq. S43, p. 9. For changing rates, the expected count is the integral \(\lambda=\int r(t)\,dt\). In a recurrent network, \(r(t)\) itself depends on past activity. The useful independence statement is therefore conditional: given the current modeled state, the elementary spike-generation noise is independent across cells in the basic 2012 model. Averaging over the evolving state can still produce correlations across time and across neurons. This qualification prevents treating a recurrent Poisson network as a collection of independent complete spike trains. Two other measurements describe different aspects of variability: The coefficient of variation, or CV, of interspike intervals, the times between successive spikes, is their standard deviation divided by their mean. A homogeneous Poisson process has exponential intervals and CV equal to one. More regular firing can have CV below one, as in the ocular motor neurons analyzed in 2022. The count variance divided by mean count is the Fano factor; its value also depends on the counting interval. CV and Fano factor cannot be substituted for one another without additional assumptions. 1.3 Mean squared displacement combines random spread with mean motion To identify where variability enters a pathway, the eye paper compares measurements that share some fluctuations and have other fluctuations of their own. For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), covariance measures how their centered values vary together: \[ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)= \mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])]. \] It has units equal to the product of the units of \(X\) and \(Y\). Variance is the special case \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,X)\). Expanding a centered sum or difference gives \[ \operatorname{Var}(X\pm Y)= \operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y) \pm2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y). \] Independence makes the covariance zero when the relevant moments exist. Zero covariance alone does not imply independence in general. The correlation coefficient rescales covariance: \[ \rho_{XY}=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)} {\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. \] It has no units and lies between \(-1\) and \(1\) for variables with nonzero variance. The magnitude of a correlation is not automatically the fraction of an output variance caused by a particular source. Establishing that interpretation requires a model of the signal, noise, and measurement gains. The eye-drift covariance calculation supplies that model for eye displacement. The quantity that changes between two times is a displacement \(\Delta x=x(t+\ell)-x(t)\), where \(\ell\) is a time lag. Its mean square splits into \[ \mathbb E[(\Delta x)^2]= \operatorname{Var}(\Delta x)+\mathbb E[\Delta x]^2. \] Thus a growing mean squared displacement can contain random spread, a systematic change in the mean, or both.
