chapters/ch-place-sizes.html: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code11 High peaks explain size laws across dimensions 11 High peaks explain size laws across dimensions A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation. Knowing the average field length does not tell us how often very small or very large fields occur. Why should the same spatial model give one size distribution on a track, another in an arena, and a third in a room? The next step is to find the shape of a typical field when only unusually high input peaks rise above the threshold. Near such a peak, the smooth input is approximately a downward parabola. Its height above the threshold sets a radius, and converting that radius into length, area or volume gives the different size laws. Cuts through a map test its spatial structure, and slopes at field edges provide a separate check on the predicted field widths. The size laws use a high threshold approximation; the boundary-slope law has a separate exact derivation under the smooth stationary Gaussian assumptions. We keep the earlier notation: \(z(x)\) is the spatial input normalized to variance one, \(q\) is its threshold, \(\sigma\) is its local distance scale, and \(a\) converts positive excess input into firing rate. The number of spatial dimensions is \(d\). The firing rule remains \(F(x)=a[z(x)-q]_+\), where \([u]_+=\max(u,0)\). 11.1 Near a high peak, the input is nearly parabolic The crossing calculation determines a mean length exactly, but it does not yet explain the shape of the length histogram. To obtain that distribution, we examine the small region around a peak that barely exceeds a high threshold. The following is a teaching reconstruction of the high excursion argument in Methods S4, with algebraic corrections made explicit below. It assumes: a sufficiently smooth, stationary, isotropic, unit variance Gaussian field; an invertible covariance matrix for the relevant derivative variables; the limit \(q\to\infty\); typical components counted once each, away from environment boundaries. It is not a proof of the full excursion convergence theorem for every allowed covariance.1 The Hessian is the matrix \(H\) of second spatial derivatives; its eigenvalues describe curvature along the principal directions. Isotropy and the definition of \(\sigma\) imply \[ \operatorname{Cov}(\partial_i\partial_j z,z) =-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\sigma^2}. \] Here \(\delta_{ij}\) is one for equal indices and zero otherwise. For jointly Gaussian variables, conditioning \(Y\) on a scalar \(Z\) of variance one gives \(\mathbb E[Y\mid Z=b]=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)b\) when both means vanish. One way to see this is to write \(Y=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)Z+\epsilon\); the remainder has zero covariance with \(Z\) and is therefore independent of it. Applying this to each Hessian entry gives \[ \mathbb E[H\mid z=b]=-\frac{b}{\sigma^2}I. \] The conditional fluctuations around this mean have a variance that does not grow with \(b\). For a high peak, the negative mean curvature is of order \(q\), so its relative fluctuations become small. Conditioning the gradient to zero does not change this Gaussian conditional mean, because the gradient has zero covariance with both height and Hessian in a stationary isotropic field. Selecting an actual maximum also weights curvatures, but its leading high peak shape is the same. Let the peak height be \(q+\epsilon\), with \(\epsilon>0\), and put the peak at the origin. The gradient there is zero. The Taylor expansion becomes, to leading order, \[ z(x)-q\simeq\epsilon-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}\|x\|^2. \] It is positive inside an approximately round region of radius \[ r_*\simeq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\epsilon}{q}}. \] The remaining question is how \(\epsilon\) is distributed when we select one high field at a time. In one dimension, the number of high maxima is asymptotically the number of upcrossings, proportional to \(e^{-q^2/2}\). Therefore the fraction of peaks above \(q\) that also exceed \(q+\epsilon\) is approximately \[ \frac{e^{-(q+\epsilon)^2/2}}{e^{-q^2/2}} =e^{-q\epsilon-\epsilon^2/2}. \] Define \(U=q\epsilon\). At fixed \(u\ge0\) and as \(q\) increases, \[ \Pr(U>u)\simeq e^{-u-u^2/(2q^2)}\longrightarrow e^{-u}. \] Thus the scaled excess height approaches an exponential variable of mean one. In several dimensions, high peak counts have the additional leading factor \(q^{d-1}\). Its ratio at \(q+u/q\) and \(q\) tends to one, so the same excess-height limit remains. The higher dimensional count factor will also follow from the Euler characteristic calculation. A rigorous conclusion requires control of the remainder and of components containing multiple peaks, beyond this local argument. In one dimension, the full field length is \(s=2r_*\). Eliminating \(\epsilon\) gives \[ s\simeq\frac{2\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\sqrt U, \qquad \epsilon\simeq\frac{q s^2}{8\sigma^2}. \] This supplies two distinct predictions: The length is a scaled square root of an exponential variable, giving a Rayleigh distribution. The peak firing rate is \(a\epsilon\), so at fixed high \(q\) it is proportional to \(s^2\). The exponent two concerns rate versus linear size. In three dimensions a suitable linear size is \(s^{1/3}\) when \(s\) denotes volume. At moderate thresholds the omitted shape fluctuations matter. Figure 3C reports a rate versus length exponent of \(1.42\) in the 200 m bat data and \(1.46\) in finite threshold model simulations. Figure 3D reports \(1.75\) versus \(1.71\) using cube root of volume in 3D. These are compatible with a model that approaches exponent two only as the threshold becomes large; they are not measurements of the limiting exponent. Figure 5A–C illustrates the progression toward simpler, usually single peak fields as \(q\) increases. Figure 4C tests this trend in the shorter bat tunnel.2 11.2 Geometry gives different size laws in each dimension A round region’s radius and its volume have different units and different distributions. This geometric conversion explains why the model predicts different histograms in a track, an arena, and a room. Let \(v_d=\pi^{d/2}/\Gamma(1+d/2)\) be the volume of a unit ball in \(d\) dimensions. For \(d=1,2,3\), it is \(2,\pi,4\pi/3\). The symbol \(\Gamma\) is the gamma function, defined for \(t>0\) by \(\Gamma(t)=\int_0^\infty u^{t-1}e^{-u}\,du\). It extends factorials: \(\Gamma(n+1)=n!\). Using the radius from the preceding section, the field size is \[ s\simeq v_d\left(\frac{\sqrt2\sigma}{q}\right)^d U^{d/2}, \qquad U=\beta s^{2/d},\qquad \beta=\frac{q^2}{2\sigma^2v_d^{2/d}}. \] The same local radius gives a length, an area, or a volume depending on the dimension of the region. Figure 11.1: In the high-threshold approximation, excess peak height fixes a radius, and converting that radius into length, area, or volume gives powers 2, 1, and 2/3 in \(U=\beta s^{2/d}\). The round regions are a guide reconstruction of the limiting geometry, not observed field shapes; see Mainali et al. (2025), Equation 1 and Supplemental Methods S4, with the parabola constants checked in this chapter. The round shape and exponential excess belong to the high-threshold limit, so they do not make every measured place field spherical. Since the density of \(U\) is \(e^{-u}\) for \(u>0\), changing variables gives \[ \begin{aligned} p_d(s)&=e^{-\beta s^{2/d}}\frac{d}{ds}(\beta s^{2/d})\\ &=\frac{2\beta}{d}s^{2/d-1}e^{-\beta s^{2/d}},\qquad s>0. \end{aligned} \] This is the paper’s Equation 1. The expression for \(\beta\) above is its leading high threshold geometric scale, not an exact finite threshold identity. A finite threshold simulation can share the approximate shape while having a different fitted scale.3 The mean and its corresponding scale are \[ \mu_s=\Gamma(1+d/2)\beta^{-d/2},\qquad \beta=\left[\frac{\Gamma(1+d/2)}{\mu_s}\right]^{2/d}. \] Derivation: normalization and higher size moments Normalization needs no special integral: \(\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1\). The same substitution supplies every positive moment, \[ \mathbb E[s^k] =\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du =\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2). \] Size has units of distance to the power \(d\), while \(\beta\) has units of inverse distance squared in every dimension. This makes \(\beta s^{2/d}\) dimensionless, and makes \(p_d(s)\) a density per unit size. These checks catch mistakes in changing variables. Writing dimensionless size as \(w=\beta^{d/2}s\) removes the size scale. The dimensional size laws then differ in shape, while the transformed variable \(U=\beta s^{2/d}=w^{2/d}\) has the same exponential law. Figure 11.2: The limiting size densities differ with spatial dimension: one dimensional length is Rayleigh, two dimensional area is exponential, and three dimensional volume has a density that rises without bound as size approaches zero, while its integral remains one. Their survival probabilities, the probabilities of exceeding a threshold, coincide after transformation to \(U=\beta s^{2/d}\), where \(\Pr(U>u)=e^{-u}\). These are exact calculations from the high-threshold limiting law, not finite-threshold simulations or measured histograms. Based on Mainali et al. (2025), main Eq. 1, p. 1111, and Methods S3. Removing units does not erase the difference between length, area, and volume distributions. The nonlinear transformation to U removes that shape difference; its shared exponential law is the assumption used in the change of variables. See Field-size laws, Eq. 1, p. 1111. Table 11.1: Field-size laws in one, two, and three dimensions. Space Meaning of \(s\) Density Consequence \(d=1\) length \(2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}\) Rayleigh; density vanishes at zero \(d=2\) area \(\beta e^{-\beta s}\) exponential; mean area \(1/\beta\) \(d=3\) volume \((2\beta/3)s^{-1/3}e^{-\beta s^{2/3}}\) Weibull with shape \(2/3\); density rises without bound near zero but is integrable A Weibull distribution has survival probability \(\exp[-(s/b)^k]\) for size \(s>0\), scale \(b>0\), and shape \(k>0\). Here \(k=2/d\) and \(b=\beta^{-d/2}\). In 3D the diverging density does not mean a positive probability of exactly zero volume; the probability of \(0<s<\delta\) still tends to zero as \(\delta\to0\). For a concrete comparison, set \(\sigma=1\) m and \(q=5\) in this limiting calculation. The mean size is \(0.5013\) m in 1D, \(0.2513\) m\(^2\) in 2D, and \(0.1260\) m\(^3\) in 3D. These values describe the same local distance scale and threshold, rather than fields with the same numerical size in different units. More generally, the geometry and moment formula simplify to \(\mu_s\simeq(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma/q)^d\). This approximation has a measurable error even for a smooth Gaussian process. At \(q=1.1,\sigma=2.4\) m, its 1D mean is \(5.469\) m, compared with the exact stationary crossing result \(3.746\) m, an overestimate of \(46.0\%\). At \(q=5\) the error is \(3.73\%\). This is why the paper compares data to finite threshold simulations as well as to limiting curves. Source check: three printed steps in the supplement The printed supplement appears to contain three algebraic errors in this calculation: Equation S18 prints multiplication by mean size where the preceding moment formula requires division. Equation S23 omits a factor \(\sqrt2\) when solving the parabola in S22 for full width. In S25 the finite-height quadratic exponent should be negative. The derivation above retains the main paper’s distributional form and obtains the constants from the displayed parabola, the moment integral, and the independent crossing calculation. These corrections concern the printed derivation; they do not establish that the simulation code or empirical fits used the same mistakes.4 11.3 Slices test spatial structure beyond field volume A model can fit field volumes and still place activity incorrectly within those volumes. Slicing the map tests that internal spatial structure. Restrict a Gaussian field to a straight line \(x=x_0+tv\). At any chosen values \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), its values are a subset of the original jointly Gaussian values. They therefore remain jointly Gaussian. Along the line the covariance is \(C((t-t')v)\); for a unit direction in an isotropic field it has the same local length scale \(\sigma\). The same argument applies to a flat plane. First slicing and then thresholding gives the same active portions as thresholding and then slicing.5 Thus a line through a 2D or 3D map has the one dimensional excursion prediction, and a plane through a 3D map has the two dimensional prediction. The field being counted is now a connected active interval or patch in that slice. One 3D component can be missed, cut into multiple pieces, or intersect several slices. The sampling rule matters. Choosing one original field uniformly and cutting through its centre is different from choosing lines uniformly through space. Large fields are more likely to be hit by a spatially sampled line, and most hits pass away from their centres. The Gaussian restriction argument describes excursions along the sampled line. The radius distribution for fields counted once each cannot be used directly as the distribution of lengths observed along a line. In the high peak picture, an isotropic \(d\) dimensional field has a radius of order \(\sigma/q\); converting this same radius into \(d\) dimensional size and then cutting it requires both hit probability and cut position. Figure 2 separates the measurements by spatial dimension: Panels A–B illustrate 2D thresholding. C measures lengths along slices, D measures original field areas, and E counts fields per observed cell. F–G show 3D examples; H, I, and J compare line lengths, planar areas, and full volumes. The dashed analytical curves change with the dimension of the measurement, even within one recorded map. The alternative spherical-field model in Figure S2 matches empirical volumes and peak rates by construction but fails these slice distributions and the topology test. Matching volumes alone is therefore insufficient.6 11.4 Why slopes at field boundaries are Rayleigh The derivative at an arbitrary position is Gaussian. A field boundary is a selected position, however, and selecting it changes the derivative distribution. Return to the crossing integral and retain only slopes between \(v\) and \(v+dv\). Their contribution is proportional to \(v p_{z'}(v)dv\). Dividing by the total contribution of positive slopes gives the slope density at a typical upcrossing: \[ p_{\uparrow}(v) =\frac{v p_{z'}(v)}{\int_0^\infty w p_{z'}(w)\,dw} =\sigma^2v\exp[-\sigma^2v^2/2],\qquad v>0. \] The height density cancels because height and slope are independent. This Rayleigh law is therefore independent of \(q\) under the smooth stationary Gaussian model, without a high threshold approximation. Absolute slopes at downward boundaries have the same law. The rate slope is \(av\), so its scale also depends on the firing rate gain. This selection effect explains why a half Gaussian law for a positive derivative sampled uniformly in space would be wrong at crossings.7 Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope \(v\), the local excursion is approximately \[ z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2. \] Its second root is \(s=2\sigma^2v/q\). Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives \(p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}\) with \(\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)\), the same constant as the peak calculation for \(v_1=2\). Figure 3A identifies which width, peak, and slopes are measured. B compares local peak counts, C–D compare rate and size, and E compares boundary slopes. The paper measures boundary slopes by a finite difference between samples 0.1 m apart. This approximates a derivative and has its own spatial resolution. It is not a direct observation of the underlying synaptic input. Mainali et al. chapters/ch-synthesis.html: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code13 Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests 13 Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests The three papers address different links between nerve-cell activity and behavior: retaining a value, producing eye movement, and representing location. This chapter compares what the models and recordings establish, and separates supported connections from further questions about how a complete neural circuit would work. A model can explain the shape of a neural code without explaining how that code is maintained. It can also explain fluctuations inside a circuit without uniquely locating the source of a measured behavior. Comparing the three papers requires keeping each claim with the mathematical or experimental test that supports it. To connect them, we first separate the spatial map, the changing represented position, and the movement measured downstream. A short calculation then shows how a common position error can make cells with different tuning change together. Comparing that calculation with each paper’s evidence and related studies identifies what a joint experiment would still need to measure. 13.1 The three papers constrain maps, dynamics, and movement For a circuit representing position, three questions arise: Spatial map: What activity pattern corresponds to each position? The place-field model addresses this question. Memory motion: How does the represented position evolve when there is no corrective input? The persistent-activity model addresses this question. Observed movement: How does a downstream physical system transform that changing signal into an observable movement? The eye-drift model combines a candidate account of memory motion with a detailed account of this transformation.1 The objects differ even when the word position appears in all three. In 2012, \(\theta(t)\) locates a network state on its attractor. In 2022, the internal eye-position command and actual eye angle are separate quantities linked through motor neurons and mechanics. In 2025, \(x\) locates an animal in an environment, and \(h_i(x)\) is a spatial input function assigned to a cell. The Gaussian process does not update a remembered \(x\) through time. The guide map gives a visual comparison of these three questions. Table 13.1: Comparison of the three models. Model Random object What determines its statistics Principal observable Persistent activity, 2012 Increments of a represented coordinate Spike variability, recurrent dynamics, tuning, neural time constants Diffusion of the stored value and readout error Eye drift, 2022 Internal command fluctuations, private motor fluctuations, and measurement noise A circuit model and the downstream filters and feedback Displacement covariance and the eye’s MSD Place fields, 2025 A function of physical position for each cell Spatial covariance, threshold, and spatial dimension Field sizes, counts, shapes, and topology The 2012 and 2022 connection is direct: neural noise can move a maintained eye-position command, which then drives muscles. The 2022 result provides evidence for a substantial shared source before the final motor neurons and shows that integrator diffusion is sufficient within the constructed model. It does not measure the circuit’s Fisher information or test equality in the 2012 bound. The place-field model describes spatially irregular tuning curves. To connect those curves to memory dynamics, we must also specify how the represented position moves. 13.2 How a static map can carry a moving estimate Suppose a network maintains a one-dimensional estimate \(x(t)\) and cell \(i\) has a fixed expected-rate function \(f_i(x)\). Its time-dependent expected rate is \[ R_i(t)=f_i(x(t)). \] Here \(f_i\) describes spatial tuning and \(x(t)\) describes dynamics. A source of time variation has entered even though \(f_i\) is fixed. Actual spike counts add another layer of variability around the expected rate. This construction is a guide calculation connecting the papers’ objects, not a model tested jointly by the three studies. Consider a short interval of duration \(t\) starting at \(x_0\). Assume that the estimate’s local displacement \(\delta x=x(t)-x_0\) has mean zero and variance \(2Dt\), and that it is small enough to linearize each rate curve. Taylor expansion gives \[ f_i(x_0+\delta x) =f_i(x_0)+f_i'(x_0)\delta x+O((\delta x)^2). \] To leading order, the change is \(\delta R_i=f_i'(x_0)\delta x\). Multiplying the centered changes for neurons \(i\) and \(j\) and averaging yields \[ \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_i,\delta R_j) \simeq f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0)\operatorname{Var}(\delta x) =2Dt\,f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0). \] This covariance concerns expected-rate changes caused by the common represented displacement, conditional on the starting position. It is not a formula for every covariance in a spiking recurrent network. It neglects higher-order changes in tuning and additional private or shared fluctuations. Near a threshold or over a large spatial displacement, the linear approximation must be revisited. 13.2.1 Example: opposite rate changes from the same position error Let the local slopes of two rate curves be \(f_1'=2\) Hz/m and \(f_2'=-1\) Hz/m. Suppose \(D=0.01\) m²/s and the interval is 0.5 s. Then the variance of the common position displacement is \(2Dt=0.01\) m². The contributions to rate variance and covariance are \[ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_1)=2^2(0.01)=0.04\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \] \[ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_2)=(-1)^2(0.01)=0.01\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_1,\delta R_2)=(2)(-1)(0.01) =-0.02\ \mathrm{Hz}^2. \] With only this one source, the two rate changes have correlation \(-1\): one rises whenever the other falls. Adding independent private noise lowers the magnitude. The negative covariance here comes from opposite tuning slopes under a common position change. It does not establish an inhibitory connection between the cells. For the same slopes, set both expected rates to 10 Hz at the starting position. The upper plot shows the fixed rate curves; the lower plot shows their changes under a common position displacement. Figure 13.1: A common displacement of \(+0.1\) m increases rate 1 by \(0.2\) Hz and decreases rate 2 by \(0.1\) Hz. The changes lie on one line. With displacement variance \(0.01\) m², their covariance is \(-0.02\) Hz² and their correlation is \(-1\). The 10 Hz baseline is chosen only to display positive rates. These are exact lines from the guide’s local example, not recorded data. Both changes are set by the same position displacement, so they occupy one direction in the two-rate plane. Independent private fluctuations would spread them away from that line. Irregular single-cell responses can therefore coexist with population changes along just one direction. To test whether a shared position error causes that pattern, one must measure how the rate changes align with the tuning curves. Field shapes alone do not supply that evidence. 13.3 Each model needs a test matched to its claim The shared-position calculation predicts how rates would change together. Establishing that connection requires measurements of those changes as well as the spatial maps. Each paper tests a different part of the proposed connection: Place-field statistics: A model that matches one distribution may have enough adjustable parameters to do so for several different reasons. The place-field paper gains support by fitting arrangement parameters and then comparing additional features, including slices and shape statistics. The separate firing-rate multiplier used in some comparisons should remain visible when counting how many quantities were predicted without further fitting. A successful high-threshold formula is also a statement about its limiting assumptions; finite-threshold simulations and the original recordings provide different kinds of checks. Eye drift: The eye paper calibrates a movement-to-firing relationship, inverts it, and compares the resulting single-neuron displacement predictions with measured displacement. Shared covariance then carries information that independent private fluctuations cannot supply under the decomposition’s assumptions. The additional MSD comparison tests the time structure: increasing stationary motor-noise amplitude cannot by itself reproduce the accumulating upstream signal. Calibration validity, source correlations, two animals, and horizontal movement remain part of the result’s scope. Memory stability: The 2012 inequality is a mathematical constraint rather than an experimental fit. Its derivation specifies what noise and dynamics it covers. An experimental comparison would need estimates of diffusion, the relevant time constants, and the appropriate instantaneous information rate, all under compatible conditions. Agreement with \(1/N\) scaling alone would not test the entire inequality, since several mechanisms can share that scaling. 13.4 Related studies change assumptions and leave circuit choices open Related studies test the assumptions and ask questions the three papers leave open: Integrating movement: The eye-position account begins with Seung’s line-attractor model. Aksay and colleagues then used recordings and perturbations in goldfish to constrain integrator circuitry. These establish the dynamical problem and experimental architecture behind the 2022 model. Neither supplies the macaque displacement-variance estimate. Burak and Fiete’s earlier grid-cell study examines path integration, updating a position estimate from movement. In its model, velocity drives recurrent population activity, and errors accumulate in the position estimate. Its accuracy ranges belong to the simulated networks and parameter choices, rather than all biological grid circuits.2 Storage capacity and changing synapses: Noise-driven storage also connects to memory capacity. Koyluoglu and colleagues ask how noise limits recall as the delay and number of stored items increase. Their comparison with human data shows why direct storage of several independent values need not capture observed behavior; transformations before and after storage alter the performance prediction. Seeholzer and colleagues examine how short-term changes in synaptic strength affect diffusion and systematic drift. These papers change the storage assumptions rather than invalidate the 2012 calculation inside its original model.3 Recordings from larger environments: For place fields, Eliav and colleagues’ long-tunnel recordings and Harland and colleagues’ large-arena recordings supply the multiple-field, multiple-scale observations. Yartsev and Ulanovsky supply the three-dimensional bat recordings. The 2025 paper reanalyzes those existing data, so its agreement across dimensions is not three newly collected experiments under one protocol. The later study by Maimon and colleagues directly compares CA3 and CA1 in large tunnels: predominantly single fields in CA3 contrast with multiple fields in CA1, while field sizes are similar. That distinction supports treating the CA1 statistics and the upstream spatial circuit as related but separately constrained parts of the explanation.4 Connectivity and learning: Gaussian spatial statistics do not identify a unique pattern of connections. Druckmann and colleagues report structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions. Bittner and colleagues show how electrical events in dendrites, the branching input structures of neurons, can induce changes in synaptic strength and form CA1 place fields. Structure and learning can therefore be present even when a random-function model describes many aggregate field statistics. The model’s success leaves open which circuit mechanism produces these maps. Input, connectivity, learning, or perturbation measurements could distinguish the possibilities.5 Benefits for perception: The source and use of eye motion are different questions. Nghiem and colleagues combine human eye tracking with a model of how eye movement affects visual signals to explain why an intermediate amount of fixational motion can help fine visual discrimination. A movement that partly originates from internal noise can still have useful sensory consequences, and feedback can regulate its statistics. Benefit for perception does not uniquely identify the neural generator.6 13.5 A joint test would compare tuning maps with population fluctuations A joint test needs tuning maps and fluctuations from the same population. A possible sequence is: Estimate the tuning maps and their uncertainty. Measure fluctuations when external signals provide little correction of the represented position. Test whether their covariance aligns with the changes implied by the tuning maps. Fit diffusion only over a range where the local approximation and measurement corrections are justified. If comparing behavior, include the physical or neural filters between the representation and the measurement. This would ask whether one system satisfies both spatial-statistics and dynamical-stability constraints. A static Gaussian-process fit alone cannot supply the diffusion coefficient. A diffusion fit alone cannot establish the distribution of fields. A joint success would be more restrictive, while a mismatch would point to a particular assumption to change: spatial input statistics, recurrent maintenance, the observation filter, or their coupling. This is proposed follow-up work, not a replication claimed by this guide. Burak, Y., and Fiete, I. R. (2012). Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons. frontmatter/ch-reading-guide.html: What the three papers establish These neuroscience papers study memory, eye control, and navigation. Their settings are mathematical models of stored values, eye-movement and neural recordings from macaque monkeys, and recordings of location-dependent neural activity in rodents and bats. This reading guide explains each study’s question, methods, findings, and limits. The subject is neuroscience: how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The three papers examine mathematical models that store a quantity such as an angle, eye movements and neural activity recorded in macaque monkeys, and location-dependent neural activity recorded in rodents and bats. They ask how activity can retain a value, how an internal fluctuation can move the eyes, and why a cell can respond at several separate locations. Variable neural signals must support reliable behavior A remembered direction must remain useful after its cue disappears; the eyes must hold an angle while an animal looks at a target; a moving animal must keep track of where it is. These tasks depend on groups of neurons, the brain’s signaling cells, whose electrical signals are brief and variable. Computational and systems neuroscience studies how these cells and their interactions support such behavior. Mathematical models connect assumptions about cells and their interactions to predictions; recordings test those predictions against neural activity and movement. Persistent activity can still lose memory accuracy Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists. The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy. The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals. Their central result is a lower bound: the uncertainty in reading the network’s current value limits how slowly that value can wander. Under the model’s assumptions, the variance of the memory error grows with storage time. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 3–6 develop the diffusion calculation, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and the limits of readout.1 Eye drift points to a shared neural source Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called fixational drift. It changes the image reaching the retina, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them. They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell’s activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement’s amplitude and time dependence. For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapters 7–9 separate the shared-drive inference, the timing of drift, and the proposed circuit mechanism.2 Smooth random maps explain the variety of place fields A place cell in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations. Each connected region of elevated activity is a place field. Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions. Their model gives each cell a smooth random function of location and allows activity where that function exceeds a threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness. The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapters 10–12 develop the spatial model, its size and shape predictions, and the tests and circuit interpretation. They distinguish exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical comparisons.3 The three contributions therefore have different meanings: a mathematical constraint on memory models, evidence about the source of eye movement, and a statistical explanation of spatial activity. Together they show how a representation can be described, maintained and related to behavior. Combining all three in one biological circuit remains a further research question, developed in Chapter 13. Starting knowledge and reading paths The guide assumes undergraduate calculus, basic probability, and linear algebra. Neuroscience terms and the required stochastic-process, information, filtering, and random-field ideas are taught where needed. The reading path builds from the signals to the models and then their tests: Chapters 1–2: establish neural signals and variability, then persistence and accumulated error. Chapters 3–6: derive memory diffusion, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and readout. Chapters 7–9: follow the eye study from shared-drive evidence through timing to a circuit model. Chapters 10–12: develop spatial maps, their size predictions, and tests of their shapes and possible origins. Chapter 13: connect the results and compare related work. For a path focused on particular papers: Memory and eye drift: follow chapters 1 through 9 in order. Place fields: read the two foundations chapters and then chapters 10–12. The spatial calculation does not require the readout derivation in chapter 6. The Glossary gives short definitions for lookup after their first explanation. Neural mechanisms and mathematical derivations answer different questions Chapters 3–6 explain how interacting neurons can retain a value while random spike timing changes it. Their treatment of the Burak and Fiete appendix separates three parts of each substantial topic: Neural mechanism: which cells and signals interact, what changes, and which features are assumptions of the model. For readout, this part also states what an observer can measure and which value it must estimate. Mathematical derivation: the general tool, its conditions, and the calculation after neural quantities are assigned to the symbols. Interpretation: what the result predicts about memory or readout, and what its assumptions leave unresolved. An equation that specifies how a cell responds belongs to the model. A derivation works out what follows from that choice. For example, a spike can disturb several cells’ activity. The circuit’s interactions remove some changes, while others leave the represented angle displaced. Linear algebra calculates which part survives; probability gives the spread of that displacement. The result then predicts how quickly memory errors accumulate in this model. The mathematical tools also apply to other systems, but this neural prediction depends on the circuit and spike statistics used in the calculation. The same distinction matters for readout. A calculation of the best possible estimate sets a benchmark under specified access to neural signals. Establishing that an animal’s neurons implement the assumed computation requires separate evidence. parts/part-mechanisms.html: Part I: Noise limits memory accuracy in continuous attractor models In a model neural circuit, the pattern of firing rates across many nerve cells can represent a remembered angle. Random spike timing can change that angle even while the circuit sustains its activity. Chapters 1–2 explain neural signals and how activity stores a value. Chapters 3–4 derive how that value wanders over time. Chapters 5–6 connect its stability to how accurately it can be estimated from the cells’ spikes. Chapters in this part Patterns of variable spikes can represent a value: Nerve cells communicate with brief electrical spikes. This chapter explains how firing rates across a group of cells can represent an eye angle or an animal’s location, and how variable spike timing affects that representation. These ideas supply the biological and probability background for the three papers. Stable representations can accumulate error: A neural circuit can sustain its firing while the value represented by that firing changes. Using eye angle as an example, this chapter separates changes in the activity of the cells from changes in the stored value. That distinction explains how persistent activity can still accumulate memory error. Spiking noise produces diffusion along the memory attractor: Burak and Fiete model a group of interacting neurons that retains a continuous value after an input ends. This chapter follows spikes through their effects at synapses and back into firing, then derives how random spike timing displaces the stored value. Boundaries and drift change memory error over long delays: In the memory-network model, random changes in a stored angle accumulate over time. This chapter extends the local spreading calculation to longer delays, where boundaries, angular wraparound, and systematic drift can change the size of the memory error. Spike information limits memory stability: A neuron receiving spikes from a memory circuit has access to information about the stored value. This chapter sets a bound on estimation error under the model’s assumptions and derives the constraint that spike information places on the circuit’s memory stability. Readout accuracy depends on how a moving memory is observed: Reading spikes from a memory circuit takes time, during which its stored value can keep changing. This chapter calculates how much longer observation can help recover the value present at a recall cue, and explains why it cannot recover every earlier random displacement.
parts/part-observations.html: Part II: Eye motion and place fields constrain different parts of a neural code The next studies connect neural activity to eye control in monkeys and to location in rodents and bats. Chapters 7–9 follow the path from a neural command through eye muscles to measured movement, and test a possible source of drift. Chapters 10–12 explain where hippocampal nerve cells fire as an animal moves and compare a spatial model with recordings. Chapter 13 asks what these findings establish together and which connections remain untested. Chapters in this part Eye drift points to a shared neural drive: Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism. Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise: Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error. A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift: A circuit that stores the intended eye angle is one possible source of fixational drift. This chapter follows the proposed model from interacting neurons through motor neurons and muscles to eye motion, and explains how delayed visual feedback can limit that motion. Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale: Hippocampal place cells fire more at particular locations as an animal moves. This chapter introduces the rodent and bat recordings, then shows how a smooth random input that exceeds a firing threshold can produce several separate active regions for one cell. High peaks explain size laws across dimensions: A place cell’s active regions can have different sizes on a route, across a floor, or in a flight volume. This chapter derives why the spatial model predicts different field-size distributions in one, two, and three dimensions, and identifies the high-threshold approximation used in that derivation. Holes and measurements test the spatial explanation: Recordings show where a hippocampal cell is active as an animal moves through an environment. This chapter tests the spatial model against the shapes and arrangement of those regions, then asks what agreement can reveal about the inputs and connections that produce them. Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests: The three papers address different links between nerve-cell activity and behavior: retaining a value, producing eye movement, and representing location. This chapter compares what the models and recordings establish, and separates supported connections from further questions about how a complete neural circuit would work.
